title: How Target Knows What You Want Before You Do

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Chapter 7 shows what happens when companies study the traces habits leave behind. Duhigg uses Target's customer-prediction work to argue that routines are not only internal experiences. They create patterns in what people buy, when they buy it, and what usually comes next. Companies can learn from those patterns and sometimes use them to predict important life changes before customers say anything directly. The chapter also explains why new products are often introduced inside familiar settings. People trust what feels normal, so marketers place the unfamiliar next to routines that already feel safe. This makes the chapter more than a business story. It is a warning that habits are legible to outsiders. The same cues and rewards that guide a person's behavior can also become tools for prediction and influence. The ethical edge is obvious: convenience and manipulation can sit very close together when companies know how to read habit patterns well.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Chapter 7 argues that habits leave readable traces, and companies can use those traces to predict and shape behavior. Duhigg's Target example shows how purchase patterns can reveal significant shifts in a person's life before the person announces them explicitly. The chapter also explains that marketers often embed new products within familiar routines because people are more likely to accept the unfamiliar when it arrives inside something that already feels normal. This is habit science applied commercially. The key point is that routines are not invisible. They generate data patterns, and those patterns can be studied. That makes the chapter morally sharper than a simple retail case study. The same tools that create convenience can also support manipulation, especially when prediction outruns a customer's awareness or consent. chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 7 asks what happens when habit science leaves the self-help world and enters large-scale commerce. Duhigg's answer is that routines create patterns other people can read. The chapter's most famous example is Target's effort to identify pregnancy-related buying behavior before customers explicitly announced it.

That example matters because it shows habits as outwardly visible. Purchase timing, item combinations, and recurring sequences can reveal changes in life stage, need, or vulnerability. Habits are no longer only what a person feels from the inside. They are also what a company can infer from the outside.

The chapter adds a second commercial move. People resist abrupt novelty. Because of that, marketers often place new products inside familiar settings and routines. A product becomes easier to accept when it arrives next to something the customer already recognizes and trusts. This is habit logic used to lower friction.

The chapter therefore sits on a moral edge. Prediction can look helpful when it surfaces relevant offers at the right time. It can also look invasive when a company knows more about the meaning of a person's behavior than the person expected to disclose. The chapter does not collapse these possibilities into one judgment, but it keeps the tension visible.

So Chapter 7 expands the book's argument in an important way. Habits are not only mechanisms of action. They are also sources of data. Once those data patterns become legible, companies can predict and influence behavior with surprising precision. The practical lesson is not merely to fear marketing. It is to understand that routines leave trails, and trails can be used. Target using buying patterns to infer life-stage change is what keeps the chapter concrete. chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 7 applies habit science to consumer prediction and influence. Duhigg's Target example demonstrates the central claim: purchase routines generate enough structure that companies can infer major life changes from behavior patterns alone. Target's analysts did not need direct confession from customers. They needed enough data to see stable signals in what people were buying and when.

This matters because it turns habits into something externally legible. A routine is not only an internal loop of cue, routine, and reward. It also leaves patterns in transaction history, timing, and preference clusters. Those patterns can become predictive tools.

The chapter also explains how marketers use familiarity strategically. New products often meet resistance if presented as pure novelty. They fare better when introduced inside already accepted routines and environments. Familiar context lowers friction. The customer does not feel that a new habit is being installed because the new item arrives embedded within something already normal.

The ethical tension is central. Predictive marketing can be framed as convenience, personalization, and efficiency. It can also become manipulation when companies use insight asymmetries to steer behavior the customer is not consciously guarding against. The Target case is unsettling precisely because the signal was real enough to outrun social disclosure.

Chapter 7 therefore changes the scale of the book. Habit knowledge is no longer only about personal change or organizational reform. It becomes a tool for reading and shaping populations. The chapter's force comes from showing that once routines become data, they become economically valuable and morally complicated. chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 7 is habit science weaponized for retail. Duhigg's Target story makes the point with unsettling clarity: enough purchase data lets a company infer major life changes before the customer says a word. Routines leave trails. Trails become models. Models become strategy.

That is the chapter's first big move. Habits are not private just because they feel private. Buying patterns, timing, item clusters, and repeated sequences create readable signals. A company that learns to read them can get ahead of the customer in ways that feel almost invasive.

The second move is familiarity. People resist raw novelty, so marketers hide new products inside familiar routines. Put the unfamiliar next to what already feels normal and the barrier drops. That is not accidental merchandising. It is habit design. The old routine becomes the delivery system for the new one.

This is why the chapter matters morally. Prediction can be sold as convenience, and sometimes it is. But when a company knows more about the meaning of your routine than you expected to reveal, convenience starts shading into manipulation. The power imbalance is not only about data volume. It is about interpretive advantage.

Chapter 7 enlarges the whole book. Habit is now population-level signal and commercial leverage. Once routines become legible at scale, they stop being merely personal patterns. They become assets in someone else's model of what you will do next. The chapter wins when you can spot the mechanism before it disappears into a story you merely admire. That is the point of examples like auditing what your purchase history reveals about your routines, noticing how apps place new features inside existing clicks, and evaluating whether convenience is masking a stronger steering attempt. They force the reader to track predictive marketing, habit trail, and familiar context in live decisions instead of cheering for the case study and moving on. The common trap is assuming the chapter claims perfect prediction. Another trap is treating all personalization as identical to manipulation. The sharper reading keeps the edge and the limit together: The chapter is about useful partial prediction at scale, not omniscient models or total consumer helplessness.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 7 changes the emotional texture of the book because it takes habit knowledge into markets, data, and asymmetry. Duhigg argues that repeated behavior leaves enough patterned evidence that companies can often infer meaningful things about people's lives without being told directly.

The Target example is powerful because it demonstrates prediction built from routine traces. Purchase timing, item clusters, and repeated combinations can reveal life-stage shifts with surprising accuracy once viewed at scale. The point is not that one purchase says everything. The point is that habits produce structure, and structure becomes legible when enough data accumulate.

The chapter adds a second marketing principle: people accept novelty more readily when it arrives inside familiar routines. A company does not always need to create a brand-new behavior from scratch. It can attach a new product to a context the customer already trusts. Familiarity lowers the friction of adoption, which means old habits become the vehicle for installing new ones.

This is what makes the chapter ethically charged. Prediction can be framed as convenience, personalization, and relevance. But the same predictive power can become manipulative when companies use insight asymmetries to guide behavior the customer is not consciously defending against. The discomfort in the chapter comes from realizing that habits are not only personal mechanisms. They are also commercially readable signals.

There is a subtle limit here too. The chapter does not say companies possess total omniscience or that prediction is perfect. Rather, it shows that even partial accuracy can matter a great deal when applied at scale and paired with strategic placement. The power lies in probabilistic leverage, not magical certainty.

So Chapter 7 expands the book into an economics of routine. Habits generate trails. Trails generate models. Models generate interventions. Once routines can be read externally, they become both useful and vulnerable. That is why the chapter feels like a warning as much as a demonstration of analytic cleverness. plan.gentle: If you work with customer behavior data, then ask what pattern you are reading, what you are inferring, and whether the use respects the people behind the signal.
plan.direct: If a work model predicts behavior from routine data, then test both its utility and its ethical boundary.
plan.competitive: If you can read the trail, decide whether you are serving it or exploiting it.

plan.gentle: If a student group or campus store notices routine peaks in engagement or buying, then ask how to use that knowledge without leaning into manipulation.
plan.direct: If a school setting has readable routine data, then separate timing insight from exploitative timing pressure.
plan.competitive: Readable pattern does not automatically grant moral permission.

plan.gentle: If you notice the same purchases or clicks repeating, then look at them as a trail and ask what they might reveal from the outside.
plan.direct: If a personal routine feels casual, then inspect the pattern it would create in a dataset.
plan.competitive: Look at your trail before the algorithm does.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Chapter 7 says habits are not only private loops. They also leave readable patterns. Target's prediction work shows how buying routines can reveal major life changes before people say them aloud, and the chapter's familiarity logic shows how new products get accepted more easily inside old routines. That is why the chapter feels both practical and unsettling.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: The chapter extends habit science into data and marketing. Repeated routines create readable trails, which companies can use for prediction, targeting, and influence. The Target case demonstrates predictive inference, and the familiarity strategy shows how existing routines become channels for new behavior. The ethical tension sits in the line between convenience and manipulation.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Chapter 7 is habit as leverage. Your routines leave trails. Target reads them to predict. Marketers use familiar routines to sneak in novelty. Once habit becomes data, it becomes power.
